args.text:
The average household's leaks can add up to more than 9,300 gallons (about 35,200 litres) of water down the drain every year, and nine percent of homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons (about 190 litres) or more a day. The usual culprits round the house are worn dunny flappers, drippy taps and other leaky valves. These sorts of leaks are often a doddle to fix, needing only a few tools and bits of hardware that pay for themselves in water saved. Fixing the easy household leaks can knock about 10 percent off your water bill.

To check your place for leaks, first you need to work out whether you're wasting water, then track down where the leak's coming from. Here are a few tips for finding leaks:

Have a squiz at your water use during a colder month, such as January or February. If a family of four goes over 12,000 gallons (about 45,400 litres) a month, there could be some serious leaks.

Check your water meter before and after a two-hour stretch when no water's being used. If the meter's moved at all, chances are you've got a leak.

Find dunny leaks by putting a few drops of food colouring in the cistern. If any colour turns up in the bowl after 10 minutes, you've got a leak. (Make sure you flush straight after the test so the cistern doesn't get stained.)

Go over the tap gaskets and pipe fittings for any water on the outside of the pipe to check for surface leaks.

Leak Detection and Flow Monitoring Gear

Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you find leaks or give you a heads-up about odd water use in a home, and cut down on water waste and the damage leaks cause. WaterSense has put together a user guide to help people get their heads around the benefits of installing leak detection and flow monitoring devices, the technology you can get on the market, and tips for picking a device and keeping it maintained to cut water waste at home. Check out the Know Your Flow and Curb Water Waste Guide to find out more about leak detection and flow monitoring devices.

Dunny Leaks

Old or worn-out dunny flappers (e.g., valve seal) can cause leaks. This simple rubber gadget holds the water in the cistern, then lets it go into the bowl when you flush. Because the rubber can wear out, the flapper should be checked every so often and replaced at least every five years to make sure it seals properly and doesn't leak. An old or worn flapper can make your dunny flush on its own or quietly leak thousands of gallons a year. Swapping a flapper is a quick and easy fix that'll save you water and the folding stuff. If you need more help, you can also ask at your local hardware shop, home improvement, retailer, or a licensed plumber. Here are some online resources from WaterSense partners:

Tip: Take the old flapper (or a photo of it) down to the hardware shop so you buy a new flapper that fits your dunny model. Keep an eye on the width of the flapper and whether it's got a foam float on it that might need replacing too. You can also check the owner's manual, if you've still got it, or the manufacturer's website for info on replacement parts.

Tap Leaks

Old, worn tap washers and gaskets are often what's behind a leaky tap. A leaky tap that drips at one drip per second can waste more than 3,000 gallons (about 11,400 litres) a year. That's enough water for more than 180 showers! There are heaps of tutorials online on how to fix all sorts of taps. Here are a few examples from our partners:

Tip: Don't forget to turn off the water line before you start!

Showerhead Leaks

A showerhead leaking at 10 drips per minute wastes more than 500 gallons (about 1,900 litres) a year. That's the water it takes to wash 60 loads of dishes in your dishwasher. Some leaky showerheads can be fixed by making sure the showerhead's on nice and tight to the pipe stem and using pipe tape to hold it. Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware shops, it's easy to put on, and it can help keep leaks under control. For trickier valve leaks in showers that drip when they're not in use, get onto an experienced handyperson or licensed plumber.

Tip: It's also a good idea to check and, if it needs it, replace the washer or "o" ring inside the showerhead while you're doing this repair.

declined.reason: Only used in the negative ('didn't give a stuff'), and as an order to the reader it reads as rude; 'keep an eye on' says 'pay attention to'.
Means a person arriving casually; food colouring appearing in the bowl takes the wrong sense.
'60 loads of dishes' is a count of dishwasher loads, not 'lots'; '60 heaps' changes the meaning.
